1.pericope_label: Who is as the wise man? a man’s wisdom maketh his face to shine: I counsel thee to keep the king’s commandment: where the word of a king is, there is power

schools.summary: Henry holds that heavenly wisdom makes a man an incomparable man, takes the knowledge of the interpretation to mean understanding the times and their critical junctures so as to direct what should be done, and compares the shining face to that of the lawgiver coming down from the mount.

Gill asks whether any son of the first man, who was made upright, can be called wise as he was, qualifies the obedience of the second verse so that it holds when the command agrees with the law of God and of the kingdom, and takes the verses upward, reading the sight one cannot flee as the presence of the King of kings and the word that carries power as the word of the Gospel.

Clarke reports that the word for interpretation is pure Chaldee and occurs elsewhere only in one prophet, that the first clause closes the preceding chapter in the Hebrew, and that the Jewish princes swore fidelity to their kings; he reads the counsel as a courtier’s rule not to meddle with state secrets, quotes the Latin motto of the despot, and observes that such governments see many revolutions without amendment, preferring the mixed monarchy of his own country; Wesley puts the face for the mind, glosses the changed boldness as roughness turned to gentleness, and grounds the obedience in the oath to keep all God’s laws.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the shining face as an intellectual and ethical transfiguration by which the educated man is discovered even in a face not beautiful, reject a rendering that doubles the brightness, insist that the duty of service is not to be thoughtlessly avoided, and note that what is said of the king in the fourth verse is elsewhere said of God and belongs especially to a despotic monarch; Ellicott takes the unconnected pronoun of the second verse for a word dropped from the text, observes that such counsels suit a writer who had lived under a despotism rather than Solomon, rejects the historic references proposed for the oath of God, and refuses the reading that makes going out of the king’s sight a withdrawal of allegiance.

debates: Is the third verse about a courtier’s manners or about rebellion? Ellicott refuses the claim that going out of the king’s sight means withdrawing allegiance, which would make the evil thing a conspiracy, since a counsel not to be hasty in rebelling, rather than not to rebel at all, is inconsistent with the context; he also rejects the alternative division of the clause. Clarke reads the whole of the first five verses as directions to courtiers under an absolute prince, and Keil and Delitzsch as a warning against thoughtlessly avoiding the service due to the king.
outliers: Clarke turns the fourth verse into political comment, observing that despotic governments see many revolutions without amendment, one tyrant rising to destroy another and then ruling as his predecessor did, and preferring a mixed monarchy after long trial.
Ellicott infers the author’s circumstances from his advice, holding that counsels of this kind suit a man who had lived under a despotism rather than the king to whom the book is ascribed.
Ellicott and Clarke independently note that the word for interpretation occurs elsewhere in the Bible only in the Chaldee parts of one prophet.

Ellicott dismisses as idle a historian’s anecdote about a ruler exacting an oath of allegiance from Jewish subjects, since the book has no connection with Egypt and the Bible itself supplies the usage.
themes: a face that shows the mind
a pronoun that betrays a lost word
advice shaped by living under a despot
power that answers to no question

5.pericope_label: Whoso keepeth the commandment shall feel no evil thing: to every purpose there is time and judgment: there is no man that hath power over the spirit to retain the spirit

schools.summary: Henry answers the sixth verse with providence, that all events with their exact times are determined in the counsel of God and determined in wisdom and righteousness together, so that the appointment is chargeable with neither folly nor iniquity, while we remain much in the dark about what is to come, since a man does not know what shall be himself and no one can tell him when or how, and therefore it is our wisdom to expect and prepare for sudden changes.

Gill allows the commandment of the fifth verse to be the earthly king’s when it agrees with the laws, or the heavenly King’s with the singular standing for the plural, and refuses to read the eighth verse of the wind, asking to what purpose that would be mentioned, and offering instead a check upon arbitrary princes who have no power over the spirits or consciences of men, or an argument for subjects who cannot restrain the wrath of princes.

Clarke takes the time and judgment practically, that discerning when and how to speak and act is a lesson for a philosopher and a study for a Christian, reads the sixth verse severely, since a man generally has opportunity to do what he purposes and his purposes are frequently evil, and reports three ways of taking the eighth verse, a paraphrase about keeping the life in the body, a set of plain maxims, and an application of the whole to the tyrant who must account to God; Wesley marks the fifth verse as a new subject and makes men disquieted by ignorance of the future.

Keil and Delitzsch hold that the commandment of the fifth verse is the king’s and not immediately God’s, since the passage treats of the ruler of a state, and reject a rendering that the keeper of it engages with no evil thing; they complain that the author of the sixth verse renders exposition difficult by repeating one particle through four clauses, and read the eighth against the man who heaps up sins until they overwhelm him, instancing the tyrant who does not know he will die by assassination; Ellicott finds the connecting particles unsolved and reports a conjecture that words have dropped from the text, preferring misery to wickedness because the clause repeats an earlier verse almost word for word.

debates: How are the clauses of the sixth verse joined? Ellicott says the connecting particles present difficulties which have not been satisfactorily solved and reports the conjecture that words have dropped out of the text. Keil and Delitzsch lay the difficulty at the author’s door, since by repeating one and the same particle through four clauses he leaves free space for taking each as confirming or as hypothetical; their own solution makes one clause parenthetical and the next a supposition. Clarke and Henry pass the construction by and read the verse for its sense.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch illustrate the powerlessness of the eighth verse from the tyrant, who does not know that he will die by assassination and whom no one can tell how it will happen, so that he might arrange for his protection.
Gill denies that the first clause of the eighth verse speaks of the wind at all, on the ground that there would be no purpose in mentioning it here.

Clarke turns the fifth verse into a rule of conduct, that when and how are settled before what, and that to discern all three and act suitably is a lesson for a philosopher and a study for a Christian.
Ellicott prefers the rendering misery to wickedness because the clause repeats an earlier verse of the book almost word for word.
themes: times appointed in wisdom and righteousness
a tyrant who cannot be warned

9.pericope_label: One man ruleth over another to his own hurt: I saw the wicked buried: because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil

schools.summary: Henry reports that many take the hurt of the ninth verse to fall on the ruled, and presses it, that rulers who ought to be ministers for good use their power to invade property and encroach on liberty, and that it is sad with a people when those who should protect their religion and rights aim at the destruction of both.

Gill keeps the tenth verse to the pomp of a funeral given to men who deserved no burial at all, turns the delay of the eleventh to account as the patience God exercises toward his own people as well as the wicked, notes that one version reads a hundred years for a hundred times, and states that the twelfth and thirteenth verses are meant to check the sinner who presumes on that patience and to make the people of God easy under the delay of justice.

Clarke says such rulers fleece the flock instead of feeding it and adds that all this relates to the despots of the East, who were despotic and are so still; he takes the holy place of the tenth verse for the sacred office held by men anointed as kings or priests, calls the word for sentence in the eleventh a Chaldee word found only in the later books, and holds that the longsuffering which leads to repentance is abused into an occasion of further crimes; Wesley makes the hurt fall on the tyrant himself, calls the throne the holy place to aggravate the trust betrayed, and finds the vanity in a glory so soon extinct.

Keil and Delitzsch render the tenth verse so that the wicked are buried and come to rest while those who acted justly depart from the holy place and are forgotten, and refuse the rendering of the twelfth adopted by several, since the particle opening the clause cannot mean although but only considering that; Ellicott locates the ambiguity of the tenth verse in a word elsewhere rendered well, prefers to translate it the same way twice so that the oppressor’s prosperity is temporary, states the ambiguity of the ninth verse without pressing it, and calls the word for sentence a Persian one found in three books.

debates: What does the tenth verse describe? Keil and Delitzsch see two classes of men, the wicked buried and at rest and the just driven from the holy place and forgotten. Ellicott shows that the ambiguity turns on a word elsewhere rendered well, which yields that reading, but prefers to render it the same way twice so that the whole verse describes the oppressor, whose prosperity ends in death, burial and forgetfulness. Clarke makes the holy place the sacred office these men held and Wesley the throne itself, while Gill keeps to the magnificence of a funeral given to men who deserved none.
outliers: Clarke and Ellicott disagree about one word in the eleventh verse, Clarke calling it Chaldee and Ellicott Persian, though both note that it occurs elsewhere only in the later books.
Clarke localises the whole passage, holding that these things relate to the despots of the East and have always been more applicable to them than to any other sovereigns.
Clarke observes that the longsuffering of God which leads to repentance is abused into an occasion of further crimes.
Keil and Delitzsch refuse the common rendering of the twelfth verse because the particle that opens it cannot mean although, but only considering that.
themes: a word that means so or well
a holy place that is a throne

14.pericope_label: There is a vanity which is done upon the earth: then I commended mirth: when I applied mine heart to know wisdom, then I beheld all the work of God

schools.summary: Henry names the perplexity of the fourteenth verse as the old difficulty of reconciling the prosperity of the wicked and the troubles of the righteous with the holiness and goodness of God, and counsels first that we not be surprised as at some strange thing, since the writer saw the just suffering as if punished for great crimes and the wicked prospering as if rewarded for good deeds, the just perplexed in their own minds while the wicked are easy and secure.

Gill is careful that the vanity of the fourteenth verse is not on the part of God, who has wise ends in it for the trial of his people or the hardening of sinners, makes the mirth of the fifteenth innocent cheerfulness and thankfulness in whatever condition, better than fretting at the prosperity of the wicked, and notes that the work of God in the last verse is not that of creation but of providence, whose steps he had viewed to find a general rule and found none.

Clarke assigns the fifteenth verse to an infidel objector and supplies his Latin motto that after death there is no pleasure, then reads the closing verses as the wise man’s reply, that God governs the world though we cannot see the reasons, that this life is a probation in which neither the wicked are punished nor the righteous rewarded, and that the man who spends his life in eating and drinking will find he has lost the time in which he might have prepared for eternity; Wesley calls the merriment sensual delight and ends with the counsel not to perplex oneself with endless enquiries but to submit quietly and live in the fear of God.

Keil and Delitzsch treat the fifteenth verse as the author’s own conclusion, met with three times earlier in the book, and dispute only whether the clause about what accompanies a man is jussive or subjunctive against several who take it as indicative; at the sixteenth they remark that a long period has formed itself under the author’s hand without a premeditated plan, halved by the conjunction in the middle. Ellicott notes that the word rendered happeneth is used in this sense in only one other place, marks the fifteenth verse as a return to a sentiment already expressed, and observes that its three words stand together in an earlier book.

debates: Who speaks the fifteenth verse? Clarke assigns it to an infidel objector whose cavils run through the book, supplying his motto that after death there is no pleasure, and reads the closing verses as the wise man’s reply to him. Wesley comes near the same reading by calling the merriment sensual delight. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott take the verse as the author’s own settled conclusion, already stated three times earlier, and Gill makes the mirth innocent cheerfulness, so that on their reading there is no objector to answer.
outliers: Clarke reads the chapter as a dialogue, the fifteenth verse belonging to an objector and the last two verses to the wise man who answers him, ending by telling the objector that his cavils are vain because he cannot comprehend what he criticises.
Keil and Delitzsch describe the sixteenth verse as a long period that formed itself under the author’s hand without a premeditated plan.
Henry states the difficulty of the chapter in its classical form before answering it, that the prosperity of the wicked has perplexed wise and good men of old.
Clarke counts three separate refusals in the last verse, that a man cannot find it out, that labouring will not help him, and that the most instructed of men will not be able either.
themes: the just perplexed and the wicked secure
